What if the interview goes wrong tomorrow? What if nobody texts back?
None of this has happened yet.
But in your head, it's already happened 【a hundred times】.
That's 【anxiety】: we suffer more in our heads than in real life.
In 1994, biologist Robert Sapolsky wrote a book: 【Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers】.
When a lion chases a zebra, it's scared too.
But once the lion is gone, it goes right back to grazing.
Humans are different. The lion hasn't come, but you've been running all night in your head.
Every time you worry, it pounces on you 【one more time】.
Sapolsky found: to your body, an imagined lion is almost as scary as a real one.
Then morning comes. No lion.
So why can't we stop? Because worrying feels like keeping watch.
The lion didn't come, so we think: 【because I kept watch】. And the next night, it comes even more.
A 2020 study: 【91.4%】 of worries in people with anxiety never came true.
But what if the lion really comes?
Then run.
Your heart races, blood rushes to your legs, so the zebra can run.
Once it's safe, it calms down fast.
Stress is made for real lions, for just those few minutes.
In your head: attacked 【hundreds of times】. On the savanna, the real lion: 【once】.
When you stop standing guard for a lion that isn't coming, you'll finally sleep.
If the lion comes, run. Until then, live fully.
Bad things happen once, at most. Don't let them happen 【a hundred times】 in your head.
If it hasn't come yet, turn off the light and go to sleep.
What lion are you standing guard for lately?
